body:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find this Qwen3.8-Flash-Next failure mode.
- [x] The issue is reproducible on the current day-0 SGLang image used by the official model recipe.
- [x] A minimal request and control request are included below.

## Description

`Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` (also reproducible with the NVFP4 checkpoint `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`) enters a deterministic token-ID-0 repetition loop when all three of these are active:

1. thinking mode (`reasoning_effort` is `low`, `medium`, or `xhigh`),
2. at least one OpenAI-compatible tool is supplied, and
3. SGLang is launched with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`.

The response starts with valid reasoning and then emits token ID `0` repeatedly. With this tokenizer, token ID 0 decodes as `!`, so the response looks like `The user wants ... tool!!!!!!!!...` until `max_tokens` is reached. No structured tool call is returned.

The same request succeeds immediately when thinking is disabled with `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false`. Without `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`, thinking works and the model emits a correct native `<tool_call><function=...>` block, but it is returned as plain content rather than `message.tool_calls`.

## Server command

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name qwen3.8-flash-next \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 \
  --reasoning-parser auto \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
  --sampling-defaults model \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 30010
```

The server logs correctly auto-detect `reasoning_parser=qwen3` and `tool_call_parser=qwen3_coder` from the chat template.

## Minimal reproduction

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:30010/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3.8-flash-next",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Call shell_probe with command echo parser-ok"}],
    "tools": [{
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "shell_probe",
        "description": "A shell probe tool",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {"command": {"type": "string"}},
          "required": ["command"]
        }
      }
    }],
    "tool_choice": "auto",
    "reasoning_effort": "low",
    "max_tokens": 32,
    "return_token_ids": true,
    "stream": false
  }'
```

Observed output excerpt:

```json
{
  "finish_reason": "length",
  "message": {
    "content": "",
    "reasoning_content": "The user wants me to call the shell_probe tool!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!",
    "tool_calls": null
  },
  "token_ids": [760, 1156, 6587, 728, 310, 1562, 279, 12168, 47460, 5224, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
}
```

## Control: non-thinking succeeds

Using the same request with:

```json
"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}
```

returns:

```json
{
  "finish_reason": "tool_calls",
  "message": {
    "content": "I'll run that command for you.\n\n",
    "reasoning_content": null,
    "tool_calls": [{
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "shell_probe",
        "arguments": "{\"command\": \"echo parser-ok\"}"
      }
    }]
  }
}
```

## Impact

Thinking-mode agent clients such as OpenCode cannot use this model's tools through SGLang. Disabling the parser exposes raw XML; enabling it makes thinking requests loop on token 0. Disabling thinking is a functional regression for this model's intended agentic use.

## Environment

- GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, SM120, 96 GB
- Runtime image: `lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:12d3392bdc8be8d35e9a95f191df6aef99c5114bdbefd41bfdc7e760e6d25ec1`
- SGLang commit in image: `d91c3682b`
- CUDA: 13.0.3
- Model: `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`
- The official BF16 model uses the same tokenizer/chat template and native `qwen3_coder` XML format.

comments.body: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36556 appears like this fixes it (tested in https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Dual-DGX-Sparks/pull/6)

Data point on the open question in the comment above: **#36556 does fix this**, at least on SM120.

I applied that PR's two resolver edits to the cookbook image at container start and then ran the exact reproduction condition from the report — thinking active, one tool supplied, `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`:

```
image   lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:12d3392bdc8be8d35e9a95f191df6aef99c5114bdbefd41bfdc7e760e6d25ec1
model   RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 @ 7b719225242aacd3dbd3f9407468c2ee9a9d2594
GPU     1x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (SM120), TP1
flags   --reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
        --quantization modelopt_fp4 --fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass
        --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass --ple-offload-embedding
```

Result — a normal tool call, no `!` run:

```
finish_reason : tool_calls
tool_calls    : [{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\": \"Oslo\"}"}}]
content       : "\n\n"
usage         : {"prompt_tokens":328,"completion_tokens":52,"reasoning_tokens":24}
```

Zero `!` characters in the content; the only characters present are the two newlines. Reasoning is active (24 reasoning tokens), so this is the thinking path rather than an accidental `enable_thinking=false`.

Caveat on scope: this is one prompt with one tool on one arch, not a sweep, and I cannot say whether the mechanism is the same one the DGX Spark reports hit — the online-softmax patch in the linked downstream PR suggests there may be more than one route to the `!` loop. But on SM120 with #36556 applied I could not reproduce it.

Reproduced on 2x DGX Spark (GB10 / SM121), serving `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` with TP=2 (image `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext`, `0.0.0.dev1+gd91c3682b`, xgrammar backend, decode CUDA graphs on) — and I can add a narrowing data point:

**There appears to be a fourth required element: speculative decoding (NEXTN / in-checkpoint MTP draft).**

Controlled A/B with everything else identical:

- **Spec enabled** (`--speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4`) + reasoning + tools + `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` → deterministic token-0 loop (`!!!!!...` inside `reasoning_content`), exactly as reported.
- **Spec removed** (same launch, the four speculative flags deleted) + reasoning + tools + `qwen3_coder` → completely clean: proper `reasoning_content` and a well-formed structured `tool_calls` entry. Repro prompt as simple as "What time is it? Use the tool." with a single dummy function.

Supporting observation: while a request is stuck in the loop, the decode log shows the draft being rejected on every step —

```
Decode batch, ... accept len: 1.00, accept rate: 0.00, cuda graph: True
```

A hypothesis that fits these symptoms: an interaction between the EAGLE-style draft/verify accept-rollback path and `ReasonerGrammarObject`'s think-end gate (`constrained/reasoner_grammar_backend.py` — `TokenSequenceMatcher` over `think_end_ids`). Multi-token accepts/rollbacks from the draft path may desynchronize the gate state so the tool grammar arms while still inside the reasoning span; prose tokens then fail the grammar mask, the mask collapses, and sampling degenerates to token 0 — which also explains the 0.00 accept rate (every draft token rejected against the broken mask).

Workaround that preserves both reasoning and tool calling (at the cost of spec speedup): disable speculative decoding when serving with tools + thinking. The previously mentioned `enable_thinking: false` workaround is then unnecessary.

Additional datapoint from a 2x DGX Spark deployment (MiaAI-Lab recipe, RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4, day-0 sglang image): on our stack the loop's trigger was **not** the conditions listed here.

## What we saw

- Intermittent token-ID-0 (`!`) repetition loop with thinking + tools — but it did **not** require `reasoning_effort` (Pi sends `enable_thinking: true` with no effort) and did **not** require per-tool `strict`.
- The loop was **state-dependent**: short single-turn requests completed fine; longer conversations (multi-turn tool loops) degenerated after a while. A 32768-max-token request with the full Pi payload (big system prompt, sampling params, stream_options) looped deterministically; the same request at max_tokens <= 16384 completed with a proper tool call.
- Each runaway (32768 tokens of `!`) took ~10 min to self-limit and **wedged the scheduler** — every subsequent request queued behind it, which made the failure look far worse than it was.

## The actual trigger on our stack

**`NVFP4_KV_CACHE=1`** (the FP4-quantized QSA KV cache, new default in the MiaAI recipe). With FP4 KV:

- thinking + tools → token-0 loop (intermittent, worsens with context length — consistent with KV corruption accumulating)

With `NVFP4_KV_CACHE=0` (fp8_e4m3 KV), the **exact same request** that looped before completes in ~7s with a correct `message.tool_calls` and `[DONE]`, at max_tokens 32768, thinking on, tools on. Verified end-to-end through Pi's tool loop.

## Suggestion

If the FP4 KV path is suspected, a quick check is to compare the same long thinking+tool request with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` vs the NVFP4 KV path. Happy to provide full repro payloads and server logs.

**Confirming #36556 fixes this on SM121 (2× DGX Spark GB10, TP=2).** Built `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` + this PR's two resolver edits. Previously a real agent-harness payload (large system prompt + 12-tool catalog) hit the token-0 loop on the first message, deterministically. With the PR applied: the exact issue repro passes, the harness payload passes, and a real 13-tool-round coding session with thinking active ran clean end to end — healthy MTP accept lengths (1.6–2.8) throughout.

One note for anyone testing on the cookbook image: with this patch alone (no downstream kernel-patch layer), fp8/nvfp4 KV cache crashes QSA sparse prefill (`Unsupported rhs dtype fp8e4nv` in the Triton `tl.dot`) — bf16 KV works. That's a separate pre-existing issue, not caused by this PR.

Config: `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, TP=2 over CX7 RoCEv2, `--attention-backend flashinfer --tool-call-parser auto --reasoning-parser auto`, NEXTN 3/1/4, bf16 KV.

Adding one more confirmation of #36556, on a different recipe stack: 2× DGX Spark GB10, TP=2 over CX7 RoCEv2, serving `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` via the MiaAI dual-Spark recipe — but with the image rebuilt as stock `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` + only this PR's two resolver edits (the recipe's local QSA Triton-fallback kernel patch removed). bf16 KV, NEXTN 3/1/4, decode CUDA graphs on.

Results: my earlier token-0 repro (reasoning + tools + `qwen3_coder`) now completes clean with a well-formed `tool_calls`; single-stream ~42 tok/s; **MTP accept len 3.95–4.00** across the run — notably higher than what I saw pre-patch.

This also explains my earlier observation that disabling speculative decoding avoided the loop: the draft-verify batches were what steered decode into the broken SM121 sparse-decode path. With this PR the spec path is clean. +1 for merging.

Additional reproduction data from 2x DGX Spark (GB10 / SM121), TP=2 over CX-7, using `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, BF16 KV, NEXTN 3/1/4, temperature 0, and the SM120/SM121 sparse-decode patch from #36556 (`dac5523`).

The request supplies one OpenAI tool, uses `qwen3_coder`, `enable_thinking=true`, `reasoning_effort=low`, `max_tokens=256`, and has 12 short prior user/assistant turns. A clean result must contain non-empty `reasoning_content`, a structured tool call with the exact requested argument, and no `!` loop.

Observed with FlashInfer autotuning enabled:

- concurrency 1: **20/20 clean**
- concurrency 4: initially 32/32 clean, but after a clean server restart one of three rounds failed as a whole (8/12 clean overall; the failed round was 4/4 token-ID-0 loops)
- concurrency 5: 20/25 clean; one complete round became token-ID-0 loops
- concurrency 6: nondeterministic; repeated 12-request thinking/non-thinking runs ranged from 4/12 to 11/12 clean, with both token-ID-0 loops and `finish_reason=length` without a completed tool call

With `--disable-flashinfer-autotune`, a thinking-only soak at concurrency 6 was **30/30 clean**, with structured tool calls and non-empty reasoning. However, single-stream decode dropped materially: median ~40.8 tok/s versus a peak of ~66.5 tok/s with autotuning enabled (the autotuned runs were variable).

This suggests #36556 fixes the SM121 sparse-decode resolver/startup path but does not fix this issue. The corruption appears concurrency/autotuner-sensitive and can disappear for many rounds before returning after restart, so a short smoke test can give a false clean result. I can provide the Python reproducer or run targeted A/B tests on this pair if useful.
Would be nice if you could share a python reproducer script @knapcio

SM121 / DGX Spark follow-up fix is now in #36845.

The remaining GB10 problem had two parts:

1. forcing SM121 through FlashInfer TRT-LLM sparse decode starts successfully,
   but silently corrupts long-context output (32/32 generated tokens were token
   id 0 at 120k, 190k, and 210k);
2. keeping SM121 out of that route falls back to FA4 CuTe varlen, which fails to
   compile QSA's packed one-query shape on GB10.

#36845 adds an exact-SM121 Triton packed-varlen fallback and leaves SM100/SM120
and other architectures on their existing routes.

Validation on one DGX Spark / GB10:

- full QSA test file: 68 passed;
- 30 BF16/FP16 differential cases: worst abs error 0.001953125, worst relative
  RMS 6.994461e-05;
- 20/20 sequential and 4/4 concurrent exact-output requests passed;
- structured `get_weather({"city":"Paris"})` tool call passed;
- exact NIAH retrieval at 120k / 190k / 210k, with zero token-id-0 outputs and
  HTTP 200 health after every request.

For the single-Spark model fit test, the PLE stayed exact FP8 and was demand
paged from NVMe; that capacity mechanism is independent of the QSA correctness
fix in #36845.

Here is the sanitized Python reproducer: https://gist.github.com/knapcio/7ae49d30d33084a6c19dc0f07401739a

It uses the official `openai` Python SDK and talks directly to SGLang's OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint. There is no client proxy, stop guard, embedded address, or credential. It reproduces the payload from my earlier comment: 12 short prior user/assistant turns, one tool, `temperature=0`, `reasoning_effort=low`, explicit `enable_thinking`, and `return_token_ids=true`.

Example:

```bash
python -m pip install openai
SGLANG_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1 \
SGLANG_MODEL=Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 \
python repro_qwen38_thinking_tools.py \
  --mode thinking --concurrency 6 --rounds 5 --max-tokens 256
```

Each result checks all of the following:

- non-empty `reasoning_content` when thinking is enabled;
- a structured `shell_probe` tool call with the exact requested argument;
- no token ID 0;
- no decoded `!` run.

For an A/B control, use `--mode both`; the control sends the same payload with `enable_thinking=false`.

Validation disclosure and results from 2x DGX Spark / TP=2 today:

- The unmodified official `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` image could not reach API readiness on SM121. During FlashInfer autotune/CUDA-graph warmup its existing FA4 CuTe QSA fallback failed with `expects coord and shape of view are weakly congruent`. No local changes were applied to that run.
- I therefore tested the official base plus only the exact two resolver edits from #36556 (`dac5523`), with BF16 KV, NEXTN 3/1/4, FlashInfer autotuning enabled, and real server-side `--max-running-requests 6`. The launch log confirmed CUDA graphs for batch sizes 1 through 6, and decode logs confirmed `#running-req: 6`.
- Thinking + tools, 5 rounds x concurrency 6: **24/30 clean**. The first round failed as a whole: **6/6** responses had `finish_reason=length`, no structured tool call, and 254-255 occurrences of both token ID 0 and decoded `!` in a 256-token completion. The following four rounds were 24/24 clean, reproducing the state-dependent/intermittent behavior.
- Non-thinking control with the same real server-side concurrency 6: **6/6 clean**, all with `finish_reason=tool_calls`, exact arguments, and zero token IDs 0.
- With the mitigation `--max-running-requests 1`, 3 rounds at client concurrency 6 were serialized and passed **18/18**, as expected.

The script does not change server configuration and prints no response text or credentials, only the structural verdict and counts.

> **CORRECTION (same day, a few hours later).** Section 2 below attributes the collapse to scheduler saturation. That reading is **backwards**, and I have log evidence now: the trigger is **zombie requests** after client disconnect (#36333 / #36876). Zombies never release their slot, so `num_running_reqs` climbs to `max_running_requests` on its own, and the `accept length 1.00` is largely the *readout of zombies decoding garbage* rather than a kernel problem. Details and evidence in [my follow-up comment](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36537#issuecomment-5455672570). Sections 1, 3 and 4 stand as measured.

---

Another 2x DGX Spark data point, and it disagrees with two things assumed above. Everything below is measured against production, not inferred.

## Setup

- 2x DGX Spark GB10 (SM121), TP=2 over CX-7 RoCEv2
- `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` @ `7b71922`, `--quantization modelopt_fp4`
- sglang built from the #36497 branch (`qwen4-main-squashed`, `73a2552`), flashinfer 0.6.17
- `attention_backend=flashinfer`, `moe_runner_backend=flashinfer_cutlass`, `grammar_backend=xgrammar`
- NEXTN 3/1/4, `max_running_requests=8`, `page_size=64`, `mem_fraction_static=0.9`, context 262144
- KV is **bf16** (`kv_cache_dtype=auto` resolves to `torch.bfloat16`), so the FP4-KV trigger reported earlier does not apply here

## 1. There are two distinct failure modes sharing the token-0 symptom

The one in the title — thinking + tools + `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` — reproduces exactly as reported and is **deterministic**. We worked around it at the proxy layer by forcing `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false` whenever the request carries tools, which is the control the issue already documents. Verified: the exact repro from the report returns a well-formed `tool_calls` instead of the `!` run.

But we also see a **second, non-deterministic** failure with the same token-0 signature that has nothing to do with the parser: it fires with no tools, no thinking, and it is what the rest of this comment is about. Conflating the two is what cost us most of a day.

## 2. The degradation is not present at startup — it appears in flight and does not recover

This is the part we had wrong for hours, because logs have no history. From our metrics backend (`sglang:spec_accept_length`, scraped from `--enable-metrics`):

```
27-08 all day        1.5 - 3.9    across SIX different pods, healthy
28-08 01:45-08:15    1.5 - 3.5    healthy for SEVEN hours
28-08 08:30          accept_rate 0.289 -> 0.000
28-08 08:30-14:30    pinned at 0.000 for six hours, never recovers
pod restart          healthy again
```

At the exact sample where it collapses, `sglang:num_running_reqs` goes from 0 to **8** — which is precisely our `max_running_requests` — with a `gen_throughput` spike to 75 tok/s. Saturate the scheduler, and the speculation wedges and stays wedged.

Practical consequence for anyone benchmarking this model: **any measurement taken after the collapse describes the wedged state, not the cause.** We falsified three hypotheses in a row because every measurement came from an already-wedged pod.

## 3. `--disable-flashinfer-autotune` did not fix it for us

Immediately after enabling it, with 8 concurrent requests:

| | value |
|---|---|
| accept length, 8 concurrent | 1.98 - 3.02 |
| aggregate throughput | 144 - 155 tok/s |
| single-stream | 52 tok/s |
| `!` characters in 8 x 400-token responses | 0 |

So it looked like a fix. It is not: the corruption **recurred later on the same pod with autotune still disabled** (accept length pinned at 1.00 across 404 consecutive decode batches in a 30-minute window). That occurrence did recover on its own, unlike the 08:30 one, so the wedge is not always permanent.

I mention this because the autotune workaround is being read in this thread as a fix. On this hardware it is at best a mitigation, and we cannot show it changes the failure rate.

## 4. Two A/Bs that came back negative

**#36556 applied: no change.** Worth being precise about why, because it may save someone else the build. With the QSA trtllm gate **open**, `_resolve_trtllm_sparse_decode` returns the trtllm function and the packed varlen fallback is never reached — so that PR's second edit (SM120 -> sglang's FA4 dispatcher) is dead code in this configuration. The PR is still the right fix for the startup path in #36531; it just does not touch our accept rate.

**QSA trtllm gate `open` vs `closed`: identical.** Both sides give accept length 1.00 and 19 tok/s on a wedged pod. We ran this specifically to test the claim that trtllm-gen decode kernels are SM100-only and silently emit garbage on SM121. If that were the cause of the accept-rate collapse, closing the gate should have changed something. It did not.

## 5. `spec_accept_length` is a usable detector

`accept length == 1.00` means 100% of draft tokens are rejected, which is the same signature reported here while a request is stuck in the loop. We alert on `<= 1.05` sustained for 5 minutes with decode traffic present (the `gen_throughput > 0` guard matters — at idle the gauge holds its last value and gives a false positive). Replayed against the episode above it fires from 08:30 to 15:00 with no false positives in the preceding healthy hours.

One gotcha if you scrape this: our pod is scraped by three jobs, so `sum()` triples it. That made us read 24 in-flight requests where there were 8 — and the 8 was the whole point.

Root cause still unidentified on our side. Happy to run targeted A/Bs on this pair if any of it is useful.

Correcting my own comment above, and I think this matters for several measurements in this thread.

I attributed the accept-rate collapse to scheduler saturation. **That is backwards.** The trigger is zombie requests after client disconnect — #36333, and its duplicate #36876 with the root-cause analysis.

## Evidence

Same 2x DGX Spark GB10 (SM121), TP=2, `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, NEXTN 3/1/4, `max_running_requests=8`.

In a 20-minute log window, **11,899 of 12,850 lines (92.6%)** were:

```
Received output for rid='...' but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager
```

Three rids, with a clear ordering:

```
16:05:57   zombie rid 5a264fd9 starts spamming
16:09:17   zombie rid 70a41588 starts
16:10      spec_accept_length collapses to 1.00      <- AFTER the first zombie
16:14:37   zombie rid 0c64f6f3 starts
16:19      #running-req: 8, accept len 1.00, all three still alive
```

The cause precedes the symptom by four minutes. The user was not issuing 8 concurrent requests — at least three of those 8 slots were requests they had cancelled, which the scheduler kept decoding.

That inverts the causality: it is not that saturating concurrency breaks speculation. Each zombie holds a slot forever, so with a few of them `num_running_reqs` pins at `max_running_requests` on its own, and `accept len: 1.00` is largely **the readout of zombies decoding garbage**, averaged in with real traffic.

## Why this is worth checking before tuning anything

It explains three things that did not fit:

- **It lasts for hours.** A zombie decodes to `max_new_tokens` and never stops.
- **Only a pod restart cures it.** It is in-memory scheduler state.
- **It appears with `#running-req: 1`.** That 1 *is* the zombie.

And a practical warning: `accept len` measured while zombies are alive describes the zombie population, not the kernel. I falsified three hypotheses in a row (#36556, the QSA trtllm gate, `--disable-flashinfer-autotune`) using measurements taken from an already-wedged pod. All three of those A/Bs in my comment above were, in hindsight, measuring the thermometer.

If anyone in this thread is tuning autotune or concurrency against accept-rate readings, it is worth checking `grep -c "state was deleted"` on the same window first. On our pod that count was 4,752 in a single 60-second sample.

## Where we are now

Running #35936 (abort pending requests before dropping tokenizer state), baked into our image. That covers the client-disconnect path, which is our case.

It does **not** cover the batch-transition window that #36876 describes in `abort_request()` — neither #35936 nor #35255 touches the `[running_batch, last_batch]` list, and I did not want to write that patch myself: in our build the invariant #29406 established still holds (nothing calls `abort_request` mid-iteration, and the mid-iteration site that PR removed is gone), so we have no evidence that window affects us, and `cur_batch` now only survives as a debug field.

Deploying #35936 is also the experiment that isolates it: with it applied, every disconnect dispatches an `AbortReq`. If a zombie still appears, the abort *was* sent and lost — which would be the first reproduced case of the #36876 window rather than a code reading. I will report back either way.

Detection, if useful to anyone: `min_over_time(sglang:num_running_reqs[20m]) >= 1` — concurrency that never returns to zero means a slot that never frees. Validated against our history: it fires exactly over the two long zombie episodes and stays quiet through the healthy stretches. I first tried `num_running_reqs > 0 and http_requests_active == 0`, which does **not** work — `http_requests_active` does not drop during the zombie window, it rises.

Two additional data points from an **RTX PRO 6000 (SM120), TP1**, running `lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext` (commit d91c3682b) with NVFP4 weights (`--quantization modelopt_fp4 --fp4-gemm-backend flashinfer_cutlass`, BF16 KV, `--max-running-requests 1`), plus our one-function local patch routing the SM12x varlen fallback to the in-tree FA4 dispatcher:

**1. The loop is not limited to thinking + tools on this build.** We hit non-deterministic token-ID-0 (`!`) runs mid long-generation with **no tools and no tool parser at all** — greedy *and* sampled (temp ≤ 0.4), thinking both on and off. Short prompts were clean; the corruption appeared after tens-to-hundreds of generated tokens, which is what made it look temperature- and setup-dependent before the decode path was identified as the boundary. Consistent with #36806's diagnosis: on this image the exact-SM120 resolver rejects the arch, so *every* QSA sparse decode step ran the packed FA4 varlen fallback.

**2. The documented workaround stack hangs decode on SM120/day-0 — do not assume it is safe here.** `--sampling-backend pytorch` alone, and the full set (`--sampling-backend pytorch --disable-cuda-graph-padding --disable-radix-cache`): server boots and prefills fine, then **zero** "Decode batch" lines with GPU utilization pinned at 100%; recovery required `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset`. Several comments in this thread used that stack for GB10/SM121; flagging so nobody reproduces our lost afternoon on SM120.

**After enabling the exact-SM120 paged-decode gate (#36806's change: add an `is_sm120()` exact-capability helper and gate `_resolve_trtllm_sparse_decode()` on sm100-or-sm120),** thinking-on generations (greedy and temp 1.0, several hundred reasoning tokens each) and structured `qwen3_coder` tool-call rounds with active thinking all ran clean — no token-0 runs, well-formed `message.tool_calls`. Throughput reference on this card: ~300 tok/s short prompts (incl. prefill), ~98 tok/s decode at 32K context.

Follow-up from the original reporter, for anyone still on a pre-#36806 image: #36806's routing fixes **much more** than the thinking+tools token-0 loop this issue was filed about. A forensic session on the same RTX PRO 6000 established that the SM120 FA4 varlen fallback also causes:

1. **Intermittent (5–19%/generation) mid-generation collapse under CUDA-graph serving with FlashInfer MoE autotune enabled** — what I had reported to FlashInfer as autotune corruption (flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4841). The MoE tactics turned out to be innocent: non-default tactics merely change FP summation order, and that bit-level noise flips borderline indexer top-k picks into gather patterns that trigger the fallback defect. With #36806's routing: 0/36 corrupt across instrumented and plain runs, at identical throughput, autotune fully enabled.
2. **50–100% of generations corrupted in `--disable-cuda-graph` (eager) serving, independent of autotune** — the same defect firing loudly. Device-level signature: full hidden-state rows of uniform bf16 `0x7fff` (fp32 `0x7FFFFFFF` as float), injected between ops while surrounding kernels' outputs verify bit-correct.

@tengotengo's observation in this thread (corruption with no tools at all on the packed FA4 fallback, clean after the exact-SM120 gate) matches this exactly — thanks, that comment is what redirected my investigation.

If you're pinned to the day-0 `qwen38flashnext` image: the one-function backport of #36806's gate in `_resolve_trtllm_sparse_decode` (accept SM120 alongside SM100) is sufficient; verified 0/42 corrupt generations across graphs/eager/instrumented arms on driver 595.84 + FlashInfer 0.6.18.
